slides: Before you practice, here's a quick summary of the topic. The three tools, how to choose numbers, and the counting tools.

slides.say: There's no fixed recipe in this topic, but three tools open almost every question. Plug in numbers, test the answer choices, and use algebra when the numbers don't decide. Numbers are usually the fastest place to start.
at: three tools open almost every question

slides.say: Read the question word first. When it asks what must be true, one allowed case where a choice fails rules that choice out. When it asks what could be true, one allowed example that works is enough.

When it asks what cannot be true, look for the one value that never works, often by finding the biggest or the smallest possible value. And not necessarily true means it fails in at least one allowed case.
at: When it asks what cannot be true

slides.say: Use only numbers the givens allow. Start with an easy one, check the choices right away, and try a number from another region only if more than one choice is left. For positive numbers, the two regions are numbers bigger than one, and numbers between zero and one.
at: Use only numbers the givens allow

slides.say: Different letters can be equal unless the question says they're different. So when equal values are allowed, try them too.

Between zero and one, squaring makes a number smaller, and the square root makes it bigger. With negative numbers, the farther a number is from zero, the smaller it is. And when the question asks for the smallest or the biggest for every x in a range, one easy number from the range decides.

Integers leave gaps. An integer smaller than twenty is at most nineteen. And if a is bigger than b, which is bigger than c, all integers, then a is at least c plus two. Use these gaps to find the biggest or the smallest possible value.

When one letter is multiplied, start from an easy pair that fits, like one and one, then put in the new value. For example, if x squared equals a cubed, x is positive, and a is multiplied by nine, then a is nine, and x squared is nine cubed, which is three to the power of six. So x is three cubed, twenty-seven, and x was multiplied by twenty-seven.

Sometimes the key is a structure from another topic. If whole numbers fit c squared equals a squared plus b squared, think of a right triangle. c is the longest side, a plus b is longer than c, and the smallest whole numbers that fit are three, four and five.

To count whole numbers from a to b: with both ends in, it's b minus a, plus one. With both ends out, b minus a, minus one. With one end in, just b minus a. For only odd or only even numbers, find the first and the last that count, take the difference, divide by two, and add one.

More items than boxes means some box gets two. To be sure, imagine the worst luck, one item in every box, and then add one more. [pause] That's it. Now go practice, and with that you've finished algebra. I'll see you in the next video.
